name: Hemifacial microsomia
aliases: first and second branchial arch syndrome

reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: The second commonest congenital facial anomaly after cleft lip and palate, characterised by asymmetric underdevelopment of one side of the face
Predominantly affects structures derived from the first and second branchial arches, especially the mandible, ear, and muscles of mastication
Ear involvement ranges from preauricular tags to microtia with atresia of the external auditory canal and conductive hearing loss
It is regarded as part of a continuum with the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and epibulbar dermoids or vertebral anomalies may coexist
Facial nerve weakness on the affected side is common owing to abnormal nerve or muscle development
The condition is usually sporadic and unilateral, though bilateral asymmetric involvement occurs
Progressive worsening of facial asymmetry during growth often necessitates staged reconstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Hemifacial microsomia is attributed to disturbed development of the first and second branchial arches and adjacent neural crest-derived tissues on one side of the face. A widely cited mechanism is early vascular disruption, such as haemorrhage or ischaemia in the developing stapedial artery territory, causing focal tissue loss that varies with the timing and extent of the insult. This produces graded hypoplasia of the mandibular ramus and condyle, external and middle ear, facial musculature, and overlying soft tissue, with the degree of asymmetry reflecting the severity of the original disruption. Most cases are sporadic and multifactorial, and the phenotype overlaps substantially with the broader oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum.
additionalInvestigations: Audiological assessment for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss
Craniofacial computed tomography to grade mandibular and ear anomalies
Ophthalmological examination for epibulbar dermoids and eyelid anomalies
Spinal imaging to detect vertebral anomalies within the spectrum
Echocardiography and renal ultrasound where systemic involvement is suspected
redFlags: Neonatal airway obstruction in severe bilateral or severe unilateral mandibular hypoplasia
Undetected hearing loss impairing speech and language development
Feeding difficulty with poor weight gain
Unstable cervical vertebral anomalies affecting anaesthetic safety
Coexisting significant cardiac or renal malformation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on severity; mild cases require limited intervention and have normal cognition, whereas severe or bilateral involvement demands prolonged multidisciplinary care with staged mandibular and ear reconstruction and hearing rehabilitation.
pitfalls: Regarding it as purely cosmetic and overlooking functional hearing, airway, and feeding issues
Failing to screen for the vertebral, cardiac, and renal associations of the wider spectrum
Underestimating progression of asymmetry during facial growth
Neglecting the psychosocial impact of visible facial asymmetry
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
management: Manage within a specialist craniofacial multidisciplinary team coordinating staged surgical and rehabilitative care from infancy
Address neonatal airway compromise and feeding difficulty early with airway support and feeding assistance where mandibular hypoplasia is severe
Correct mandibular hypoplasia and asymmetry with staged reconstruction such as mandibular distraction osteogenesis or costochondral rib grafting, alongside orthodontics
Rehabilitate hearing early with bone-conduction hearing aids and undertake ear reconstruction, whether microtia repair or prosthesis, at an appropriate age
Manage epibulbar dermoids, eyelid anomalies and facial-nerve weakness with ophthalmology and reconstructive input
Monitor facial growth and screen for vertebral, cardiac and renal involvement within the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum
Offer genetic counselling, noting that most cases are sporadic
